query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered suitable for thin-film use, and its expense favors applying it as a protective coating on conventional metals rather than using it in bulk. Earlier studies examined room-temperature wear behavior in relation to coating–substrate combinations, composition, and grain size, but largely addressed the alloy itself or a limited thermal regime rather than the overall wear response of a coating across different temperatures. Under the constraints that FeNiCrCoCu remains a thin protective coating and that high-temperature wear is the target application, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its overall wear resistance and why? Specify an intervention relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, state the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The wear resistance of FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings is governed by the formation of a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer at high temperatures, which minimizes adhesive and oxidative wear.
generation.material_initial_state: FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coating on a conventional metal substrate
generation.intervention: Annealing the coating at 800 °C for 30 min to promote the formation of a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer
generation.conditions: High-temperature wear testing (up to 800 °C) with a sliding speed of 0.1 m/s and a normal load of 10 N
generation.mechanism: The formation of a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer at high temperatures reduces the coefficient of friction and minimizes adhesive and oxidative wear, leading to improved wear resistance
generation.predicted_outcome: The annealed FeNiCrCoCu coating will exhibit a lower wear rate and coefficient of friction compared to the as-deposited coating at high temperatures
generation.boundary: Temperature range: up to 800 °C, loading range: up to 10 N
generation.uncertainty: The exact mechanism of glaze layer formation and its effect on wear resistance is not fully understood and requires further investigation

falsification_experiment.design: Reciprocating sliding wear test with a ball-type friction tester
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed FeNiCrCoCu coating exhibits a higher wear rate and coefficient of friction compared to the as-deposited coating at high temperatures, the hypothesis is falsified

## Abstract
AbstractSustained wear damages on the sliding surfaces of alloys are generally the culprit responsible for the failure of various mechanical systems. Inspired by high-entropy effects, here we deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 complex concentrated alloy, which yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C. Such remarkable wear resistance heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for the bulk alloys or composites, and originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates. This cooperative heterostructure releases gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear at room temperature through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways while activating a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer upon wear at 800 °C to minimize adhesive and oxidative wear. Our work uncovers a practical avenue for tailoring wear properties with multicomponent heterostructures over a wide temperature range.
